Carl Benedikt Frey, Giorgio Presidente (earlier working-paper version with Chinchih Chen)
Privacy regulation and firm performance: Estimating the GDPR effect globally
Difference-in-differences by firm exposure to EU markets with firm and country-industry-year fixed effects

GDPR lowered the profitability of firms targeting European consumers through a cost channel: technology firms saw a 2.1% decline in profits but not in sales; GDPR raised extra expenses and wage bills, accelerated patenting in GDPR-related fields, and burdens fell mainly on smaller firms.
GDPR and the Lost Generation of Innovative Apps
Event study of app exit and entry around GDPR plus a structural model of demand and entry for counterfactual equilibria

GDPR induced the exit of about a third of available apps and halved new app entry in the following quarters; in the long-run counterfactual GDPR reduces consumer surplus and aggregate app usage by about a third.
Colleen Cunningham, Florian Ederer, Song Ma
Theory plus difference-in-differences comparing development of acquired drug projects that overlap vs do not overlap with acquirer's portfolio

Acquired projects are less likely to be developed when they overlap with the acquirer's portfolio, especially where the acquirer has market power; conservatively 5.3%-7.4% of acquisitions in the sample are killer acquisitions.
Sai Krishna Kamepalli, Raghuram Rajan, Luigi Zingales
Theoretical model of platform competition, app developer adoption and VC financing under expected acquisition

The prospect of quick acquisition by an incumbent platform reduces app developers' incentive to adopt an entrant, lowering the entrant's stand-alone value and acquisition price, and so reducing VC incentives to fund entry: a 'kill zone' around incumbents.
Regulation, productivity and growth: OECD evidence
Industry-level panel regressions of multifactor productivity growth on OECD product market regulation and privatisation indicators, with a catch-up-to-frontier specification

Reforms promoting competition and private governance are associated with faster productivity growth; in manufacturing, liberalisation gains are larger the further a country is from the technology leader, suggesting entry-limiting regulation slows technology adoption. Strict product market regulation and lack of reform appear to underlie the weak productivity of some continental European countries.
Renaud Bourlès; Gilbert Cette; Jimmy Lopez; Jacques Mairesse; Giuseppe Nicoletti
Do Product Market Regulations in Upstream Sectors Curb Productivity Growth? Panel Data Evidence for OECD Countries
Endogenous-growth model tested on an industry panel; MFP growth regressed on regulation in supplier (upstream) sectors weighted by input-output links, interacted with distance to frontier
Anticompetitive upstream regulations significantly curbed MFP growth over the preceding fifteen years, more strongly for observations close to the productivity frontier.
Jens Arnold; Giuseppe Nicoletti; Stefano Scarpetta
Regulation, Allocative Efficiency and Productivity in OECD Countries: Industry and Firm-Level Evidence
Industry allocative-efficiency (Olley-Pakes covariance) comparisons and firm-level productivity regressions interacting service regulation with ICT-use intensity and distance to frontier

Resources were allocated less efficiently across firms where service regulation was less market-friendly; anti-competitive service regulation hampered productivity growth in ICT-using sectors, especially for firms catching up to or near the technology frontier.
Alberto Alesina; Silvia Ardagna; Giuseppe Nicoletti; Fabio Schiantarelli
Sector-country panel regressions of investment on time-varying OECD regulation indicators (entry barriers, public ownership), with fixed effects and GMM
Various measures of product market regulation, particularly entry barriers, are robustly and negatively related to investment; reforms that liberalise entry are very likely to spur investment.
Macroeconomic Effects of Regulation and Deregulation in Goods and Labor Markets
General-equilibrium model with monopolistic competition in goods markets and wage bargaining in labour markets; regulation sets entry costs, competition and worker bargaining power

Deregulation reduces and redistributes rents; even if beneficial in the long run, it can bring incumbent decline, temporarily higher unemployment and lower real wages. Product market deregulation can make labour market deregulation politically easier.
Bart van Ark; Mary O'Mahony; Marcel P. Timmer
The Productivity Gap between Europe and the United States: Trends and Causes
Growth accounting with EU KLEMS industry data decomposing labour productivity into ICT capital, other capital, labour quality and MFP

Since the mid-1990s US labour productivity growth accelerated while Europe's slowed; the gap reflects slower emergence of the knowledge economy in Europe (lower ICT investment contributions, a small ICT-producing sector and slower MFP growth), concentrated in market services, with labour market functioning and high product market regulation as underlying issues.
Nicholas Bloom; Raffaella Sadun; John Van Reenen
Americans Do IT Better: US Multinationals and the Productivity Miracle

Compares US-owned, other multinational and domestic establishments operating under the same European regulations; event study of takeovers by US vs non-US multinationals; links to management practices survey

US multinationals in Europe obtained higher productivity from IT than non-US multinationals, and establishments taken over by US multinationals (but not others) raised the productivity of their IT; the US IT-related productivity advantage is primarily due to tougher 'people management' practices.
Dan Andrews; Chiara Criscuolo; Peter N. Gal
The Best versus the Rest: The Global Productivity Slowdown, Divergence across Firms and the Role of Public Policy
Tracks productivity of global frontier vs laggard firms; regressions of the frontier-laggard gap on sectoral product market reform intensity

Labour productivity at the global frontier grew 2.8% a year in manufacturing in 2001-2013 versus 0.6% for non-frontier firms, with an even wider gap in market services; divergence was stronger in industries where product market reforms were least extensive.
The future of European competitiveness (Part A: A competitiveness strategy for Europe)
Policy diagnosis drawing on macro comparisons, sector studies and stakeholder input

Real disposable income per capita has grown almost twice as much in the US as in the EU since 2000; around 70% of the per capita GDP gap with the US at PPP (which rose from 31% in 2002 to 34%) is explained by lower productivity. The EU has around 100 tech-focused laws and over 270 regulators active in digital networks, and many EU laws take a precautionary ex ante approach that the report says hampers innovation.
From laggard to leader? Closing the euro area's technology gap
Speech synthesising ECB staff and academic research

Big-four euro area labour productivity rose from 25% of the US level in 1945 to 100% in 1995, then fell back to about 0.8 by 2008; US services productivity grew 3.2% a year in 1995-2005 versus 0.9% in Europe. She cites evidence that strict product market regulation, rigid labour markets and red tape inhibited digital adoption, and that intra-EU services trade is only about 15% of GDP versus over 50% for goods because of remaining regulatory barriers.
Regional Economic Outlook: Europe, October 2024 (and 'Europe's Productivity Weakness: Firm-Level Roots and Remedies', IMF WP/25/40)
Structural gravity model comparing cross-border with domestic trade flows; residual trade costs converted to ad valorem tariff equivalents

Intra-EU trade costs in 2020 were equivalent to an ad valorem tariff of about 44% for the average manufacturing sector (vs about 15% between US states) and about 110% for services. The working paper finds smaller markets and limited market-based finance are key bottlenecks for Europe's frontier firms.
European Parliamentary Research Service (Joseph Dunne et al.)
Europe's two trillion euro dividend: Mapping the Cost of Non-Europe, 2019-24
Compilation of sectoral 'cost of non-Europe' estimates of gains from adopting and implementing Parliament-backed EU policies
Potential gains of over EUR 2.2 trillion (about 14% of 2017 EU GDP) if Parliament-backed policies were adopted and fully implemented over 2019-2029, measured mainly as additional GDP.
Thierry Mayer; Vincent Vicard; Soledad Zignago
Structural gravity estimation of EU single market trade creation versus ordinary regional trade agreements, then general-equilibrium counterfactuals (shallow RTA or WTO rules, with/without Brexit)

Working-paper version: the Single Market raises bilateral trade more than three times as much as a typical regional trade agreement, and the trade-related cost of non-Europe is about 3% to 7% of GDP on average depending on the counterfactual, largest for small open (especially Eastern) economies.
Die Betriebe mussten in den letzten drei Jahren 325.000 Arbeitskräfte zusätzlich einstellen, um die gewachsene Bürokratie zu bewältigen
Firm survey (IAB Job Vacancy Survey Q1 2025, 9,209 establishments), self-reported

Average perceived bureaucracy burden rose by more than one point (to 6.8 of 10) in three years; 11% of establishments hired extra staff to cope (about 325,000 workers); 80% report higher costs, 55% productivity losses, 15% competitive disadvantages, 19% investment and 16% innovation obstacles (30% among large firms). The GDPR is named most often as a burden (68%), followed by EU IT-security rules (32%).
Transatlantic Technologies: The Role of ICT in the Evolution of U.S. and European Productivity Growth
Industry-level growth accounting with EU KLEMS data

Most of the 1995-2005 US productivity revival came from ICT-intensive industries producing market services and computer hardware; the EU-10 instead slowed 'due to a paucity of ICT investment, a failure to capture the efficiency benefits of ICT, and performance shortfalls' in ICT production, finance-insurance, retail-wholesale and agriculture. Much of ICT's effect ran through spillovers to TFP. Both regions slowed after 2005.
Sectoral productivity vis-à-vis the US and heterogeneity within the EU27: the role of firm size distribution and firm demographics
Cross-country, cross-sector regressions of productivity levels and growth on technology, innovation, capital, firm size distribution and firm demographics

The EU27 keeps a large negative productivity gap with the US and strong heterogeneity across Member States. Findings point to improving technological adoption, raising innovation intensity, boosting human, tangible and intangible capital, eliminating barriers to growth in firm size and easing firm entry and exit; these matter even more in business services.
Andrew B. Hall; Anna Le Sun
Investing in Political Expertise: The Remarkable Scale of Corporate Policy Teams
Classification of job titles of about 100 million workers (LinkedIn/Revelio data, 100,000+ job listings), merged with lobbying records for 10,000 firms

More than 250,000 people work in corporate policy roles in the US; policy teams are very roughly 13 times larger than lobbying teams and have grown relative to other corporate positions over two decades. The average firm has about 1.5 policy staff and 0.68 lobbyists; the average Fortune 100 firm has about 52 policy staff and 18 lobbyists. Lobbying and policy teams are complements.
